new_statements.quote: § 11. Pre-penultimate Vowels : I. In the Initial Syllable : The initial syllable in OM. being accented usually does not change qualitatively. Quantitatively, however, it is liable to change [...] [§ 9, p. 17:] These final vowels in MI-A. were pronounced with very little accent as is shown by the literary Apabhraṁśa in which the final o of the nom. sg. of masculine nouns ending in a becomes u, though not regularly. Naturally, in course of time, these weak final vowels were lost in all NI-A. languages, with some exceptions. Marathi followed the general trend and dropped the final vowel

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tulpule assumes the word-initial syllable of Old Marathi carried the accent (hence its vowel keeps its quality), while old final vowels were weakly accented and lost; no explicit rule for a primary stress position beyond this, and no accent section.
new_statements.exceptions: Initial vowels may still change in quantity (a > long a in heavy/open syllables; i, u short in polysyllables, long in disyllables, shortened in compounds); some initial vowels exceptionally altered (e.g. etha < atra); loose OM orthography blurs length.
new_statements.domain_note: Extinct literary language (c. 1000-1350) known only from inscriptions and manuscripts; accent is never written, so the statement is an inference used to explain vowel preservation, not an observation. Bloch 1914/1920 secs. 32-36 (the standard comparative grammar, on file) explicitly holds that no accent is proven for the old period, calls the (old penult >) Marathi final syllable the 'sommet rythmique du mot', and treats the vowel changes as purely quantitative rhythm, so the two open sources point in different directions (initial prominence vs. final rhythmic peak / no stress).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe literary/inscriptional Old Marathi of c. 1000-1350 (Yadava period: inscriptions, Jnanesvari 1290, Mahanubhava prose), i.e. Glottolog oldm1244 / ISO omr. Bloch's secs. 32-36 concern the Prakrit-to-Marathi development generally and his sec. 34 remarks (Joshi, Navalkar) are about modern Marathi (mara1378), not Old Marathi.

sources.note: English translation of secs. 32-36 (same content as the French): accent not proven for the old period; history of accent 'can not be construed in a continuous manner'; purely quantitative rhythm.

sources.citation: Bloch, Jules. 1914 [reissued 1920, BEHE 215]. La formation de la langue marathe. Paris: Champion. (archive.org IA41549913_0018; hard link from maha1305)
sources.note: Secs. 32-36 pp. 50-53: old penult became the Marathi final syllable and 'le sommet rythmique du mot'; 'la presence d'un accent n'est pas prouvee pour la periode ancienne'; modern descriptions uncertain (Joshi penult/long final; Navalkar even tone, initial slightly raised); treats vowel developments as 'un rythme purement quantitatif', rejecting the penult-stress + initial counter-accent account.

sources.citation: Rajvade, V. K. 1909, ed. S. G. Tulpule 1979. Jnanesvarici prastavana ani Jnanesvaritil marathi bhasece vyakaran. Mumbai: Maharashtra Rajya Sahitya ani Samskrti Mandal. [Marathi] (archive.org wg359)
sources.note: No accent section found; only an incidental remark p. 215 that geminate ll occasionally appears in the Jnanesvari 'svaraghatartha' (for accent), e.g. pahalla.
